name: Metolazone

lead: Metolazone is a potent thiazide-like diuretic used for edema from heart failure, kidney disease and liver disease, and sometimes for high blood pressure. Clinicians often pair it with a loop diuretic when the loop diuretic alone is insufficient.
It appears in this wiki as a strong water pill. No study has tested it for facial puffiness or other cosmetic aims.

paras: It blocks the sodium-chloride symporter in the distal convoluted tubule, so less sodium and water return to the blood. It remains active at lower kidney function than most thiazides and is described as about ten times as potent as hydrochlorothiazide.[1]

Fluid loss can cause low blood pressure, and electrolyte imbalances (low sodium, potassium, chloride, magnesium; high calcium and uric acid) are common concerns. Rare serious effects include aplastic anemia, agranulocytosis, pancreatitis and angioedema. It is prescription-only.[1]

lead: Metolazone is a thiazide-like diuretic sold as Zaroxolyn, Zytanix, Mykrox and Metoz. It was patented in 1966 and approved for medical use in 1974.[1] It treats edema from heart failure, kidney disease and cirrhosis and is used for hypertension, though hydrochlorothiazide is more commonly used for blood pressure.[1]

Its characteristic role is as an add-on to loop diuretics such as furosemide to overcome diuretic resistance in heart failure.[1][2] Trials of add-on strategies, including MELT-HF, have examined this use.[3][4]
No published research has examined metolazone for cosmetic purposes.

paras: Metolazone treats edema from heart failure, kidney disease, nephrotic syndrome and cirrhosis and is used for hypertension. It is often combined with a loop diuretic and stays active at lower kidney function than most thiazides.[1][5]

A 1994 randomised trial examined combination diuretic treatment in severe heart failure.[2] The 3T trial compared strategies for loop diuretic resistance in acute heart failure.[3] A pilot trial of early metolazone add-on (MELT-HF) was terminated.[4]

Fluid loss can cause low blood pressure, dizziness and headache, and electrolyte imbalances are common. Rarer events include aplastic anemia, agranulocytosis, pancreatitis and angioedema; it can unmask diabetes or worsen gout, and people with sulfa allergies may react.[1]
About 65% of an oral dose reaches the bloodstream, with a half-life near 14 hours; about 80% is excreted in urine.[1]

Metolazone was patented in 1966 and approved in 1974; Wikipedia credits chemist Bola Vithal Shetty with its development and says it became popular partly because it appeared less harmful to the kidneys in chronic kidney disease.[1]
Metolazone is listed among WADA-prohibited substances on Wikipedia.[1] The sources reviewed contain no substantive discussion of it in looksmaxxing communities.
No studies found on metolazone for facial depuffing or other appearance goals. Heart-failure trials include a randomised combination-diuretic study and the 3T trial.[2][3]
